Global Homicide Rate Overview

Trajectory of intentional homicide rates worldwide, 1990–2023

Over the three-decade observation window, the global median intentional homicide rate has been declining, with an overall change of -45.1% from 1990 to 2023. The global median rate across all countries' latest available years stands at 2.58 per 100,000 population, compared to a mean of 7.47 — a meaningful gap that reflects the influence of high-rate outlier countries skewing the average upward.

The chart below tracks both the median and mean rates alongside the number of countries reporting each year. A critical observation: the apparent shifts in global averages are partly artifacts of which countries are reporting in any given year, particularly in the early 1990s when coverage was lower. As reporting expanded through the 2000s and 2010s, the measured global rate should be interpreted accordingly.

Figure 1: Global median (blue) and mean (orange dashed) homicide rates per 100,000 population, overlaid with annual country count (bars). Source: UNODC CTS.
Headline finding: The global homicide rate is broadly declining over the observation period. The decade-over-decade comparison reveals: 1990s average 8.27 → 2000s 8.51 (+2.9%) → 2010s 7.70 (-9.6%) → 2020–2023 7.71 (+0.2%).

Regional & Country-Level Comparison

Geographic patterns of homicide concentration

Homicide is profoundly unequal in its geographic distribution. The regional trend analysis reveals that the Americas consistently record the highest median homicide rates, driven by Central America, the Caribbean, and parts of South America. Europe and Oceania maintain among the lowest rates globally, while Asia and Africa occupy intermediate positions with significant intra-regional variation.

Figure 2: Median homicide rate trends by region (1990–2023). Each line represents the median of country-level rates within the region.
Interpretation caution: Regional medians reflect only the countries with available data in each year. Regions with fewer reporting countries — particularly Africa in the 1990s — may understate true rates due to selection effects in national reporting capacity.

Gender Disparity in Homicide Victimization

Male-to-female victimization ratios and their evolution

One of the most consistent and striking patterns in homicide data is the substantial over-representation of male victims. Globally, the median male-to-female homicide rate ratio stands at 3.18× — meaning males are, on average, roughly 3.18 times more likely than females to be victims of intentional homicide. This disparity persists across all regions and time periods in the dataset, though its magnitude varies considerably by geography.

This gender gap is not uniform: in some regions and country contexts, female homicide rates approach or occasionally exceed male rates, often linked to intimate partner violence and femicide patterns that may be categorized differently across national reporting systems. Analysts should note that gender-disaggregated data is less consistently available than the aggregate "both" category.

Figure 5: Left — Global median homicide rates for male and female victims (1990–2023). Right — Male-to-female ratio over time. Source: UNODC CTS.
Figure 6: Median male-to-female homicide rate ratio by region (latest available year per country). Bars to the right of the reference line (1.0) indicate male over-representation.
Policy implication: The persistently high M/F ratio (3.18×) indicates that male victimization is a dominant driver of overall homicide levels. Effective prevention strategies must address the specific risk factors facing young men — including gang involvement, interpersonal conflict, and economic marginalization — while maintaining dedicated attention to femicide and intimate partner violence, which disproportionately affect female victims.
4

Age Group Analysis

Which age cohorts face the greatest homicide risk?

Age-disaggregated analysis reveals that homicide victimization is heavily concentrated among working-age adults, with the 15–29 and 30–44 age groups recording the highest median rates globally. Youth — particularly adolescents and young adults — face disproportionately elevated risk, a pattern consistent across regions and documented extensively in violence prevention literature.

Children (0–14) and older adults (60+) generally exhibit lower rates, though this varies by country context. In high-violence settings, all age groups may face elevated risk, while in low-violence settings, the concentration in young adult cohorts is especially pronounced as a relative share of all homicides.

Figure 7: Left — Median homicide rate by age group (global, pooled). Right — Age group rate trends over time. Note: coverage of age-disaggregated data varies significantly by country and year.
Data coverage note: Age-disaggregated data is considerably less complete than the overall aggregate. Standard age bands (0–14, 15–29, 30–44, 45–59, 60+) are not uniformly reported by all countries, and groupings may differ. Trends here reflect the subset of countries with consistent age-band reporting.

Notable Country-Level Trends & Outliers

Dramatic improvements and deteriorations over the observation period

Beneath the global averages lie countries with remarkable trajectories — both positive and concerning. The analysis below identifies countries whose homicide rates changed most dramatically (by percentage) between their earliest and latest observation periods. These outliers are essential for understanding what drives change and where interventions have succeeded or failed.

6

Data Limitations & Policy Recommendations

Transparency on data quality and evidence-based actions
Figure 9: Data coverage by region and decade — number of countries reporting homicide data. Earlier decades, especially in Africa, show significantly lower coverage.

Known Data Limitations

  • Unbalanced panel: Not all countries report for every year. The set of reporting countries changes over time, meaning global averages are not computed over a fixed set of nations. Early-period statistics (especially pre-2000) cover fewer countries and should be compared cautiously to later periods.
  • No interpolation: Missing country-years are simply absent — no imputation was performed. Gap-filling methods could produce misleading trend estimates and are not used here.
  • United Kingdom caveat: UK figures refer to England and Wales only; Scotland and Northern Ireland report separately. Treat UK-level statistics accordingly when making sub-national comparisons.
  • Territories vs. countries: Some territories (Hong Kong, Puerto Rico, Macao) are included separately. These should not be aggregated with parent-country data to avoid double-counting.
  • Classification differences: "Intentional homicide" definitions and classification practices vary across national legal systems and over time. Cross-country comparisons should acknowledge this definitional heterogeneity.
  • Age-band inconsistency: Standard five-year age bands are not uniformly reported. Age-disaggregated findings reflect a non-representative subset of reporting countries.
  • Reporting capacity bias: Countries with strong statistical systems are more likely to appear in the dataset. High-conflict or low-capacity states — where homicide may be most severe — are often underrepresented, potentially understating global burden.

Policy Recommendations

1. Prioritize youth violence prevention

The 15–29 age group bears disproportionate homicide risk. Targeted programs addressing youth unemployment, gang recruitment pathways, and community-level risk factors are essential in high-burden contexts.

2. Strengthen gender-responsive strategies

The 3.18× male-to-female victimization ratio demands interventions specifically addressing male risk factors, while dedicated femicide and intimate partner violence programs must be resourced in parallel.

3. Invest in statistical reporting capacity

Coverage gaps — especially in Africa and conflict-affected states — limit the ability to monitor and respond to homicide trends. International support for national statistical systems is a foundational policy investment.

4. Learn from successful decreases

Countries demonstrating sustained rate reductions offer model evidence for effective interventions. Systematic documentation and transfer of successful approaches can accelerate progress in high-burden settings.

5. Focus resources on the Americas hotspots

Regional analysis consistently identifies Central America and the Caribbean as the highest-burden areas. Targeted international cooperation, security sector reform, and social investment in these regions offer the greatest potential for global rate reduction.

6. Harmonize data standards internationally

Definitional inconsistencies in homicide classification undermine comparability. Adoption of standardized UNODC reporting templates and regular peer review of national statistics would strengthen the evidence base.

Data Source: UNODC Crime Trends Survey (CTS), accessed via Kaggle dataset "Global Homicide Rates by Country" (lucalullo/global-homicide-rates-by-country). Dataset spans 1990–2023 across 201 countries with 22,092 observations.
Analysis scope: All figures derived directly from the provided dataset. No external statistics, imputed values, or fabricated data were used. Reported values represent rates per 100,000 population.
Caveats: This report reflects available data as of the dataset's last update. Coverage is uneven across countries and years; findings should be interpreted in light of the data limitations described in Section 6.

Prepared for policy analysts and public safety stakeholders. Not for attribution without independent verification against primary UNODC sources.
